title: Turn an idea into a useful result
subtitle: Choose a result you can explain and a first version you can check.

coursePath: Turn an idea into a useful result
Decide whether to trust the report
Make it work for your needs

sections.title: See where the work went
sections.intro: Six activity entries can answer a useful question: how much time went to each project and category?
sections.html:
Click Open formatted report. Find the total, one project and one category. A readable report lets you explain where the time went without adding every row again.

The target result from the six supplied rows
Entries6
Total270 minutes, or 4 hours 30 minutes
ProjectsOrion 180 minutes; Lumen 90 minutes
CategoriesDevelopment 150; Documentation 75; Testing 45 minutes

In this course, you direct the outcome and decisions. Your assistant helps inspect the project and prepare the work. Harness retains the agreed request, checks and execution evidence for supported workflows.

Start by defining what would make the report useful. You do not need to design its code. Opening the supplied report does not mean that you have built a new one.
presenterNotes: Show the useful report before explaining workflow terms. Ask the learner to locate one value they care about.
Use the current supplied report and current checks summary. Opening an example is different from the learner completing a new task.

sections.title: Check the six entries
sections.intro: The projects and activity are synthetic. The small input makes the target result easy to check yourself.
sections.html:

Read the actual activity CSV, which also includes the dates. Add Orion's rows: 90 + 30 + 45 + 15 = 180 minutes. Lumen has 60 + 30 = 90 minutes. Together they account for 270 minutes, or 4 hours 30 minutes.

Pick a category and add its rows before looking at the report. Development should total 150 minutes, Documentation 75 and Testing 45. These expected answers come from the input, not from trusting the reporting code.
presenterNotes: Let the learner work through one total in their own way. No arithmetic speed or coding skill is being assessed.
Read the linked CSV if a displayed table and source disagree. Preserve the synthetic fixture.

sections.title: Describe what the person needs
sections.intro: A good goal explains the useful result. It does not force you to specify the implementation.
sections.html:
A clear reporting goal

Turn the supplied activity CSV into a readable report so a person can explain total time by project and category without manually adding the rows.

That goal tells the assistant why the report matters. It also gives you a way to assess the result: can a reader find the totals and connect them to the input?

  1. Name the input: the supplied synthetic CSV.
  2. Name the reader's useful result: understand where the time went.
  3. Name what the output must show: entry count, total minutes, project totals and category totals.
  4. Ask what remains unclear before accepting the work.

Your assistant can recommend an approach and explain its tradeoffs. You settle choices that change the result, such as the intended reader or output format.

Choose your starting path: this bounded reporting exercise starts from a clear goal. If your real project has several workflows or unresolved requirements, use the goal-driven and spec-driven reference to choose the preparation it needs before accepting a plan.

copies.label: goal prompt
copies.text: Help me define a useful reporting task from the supplied synthetic activity CSV. The reader should understand where the time went without manually adding the rows. Inspect the input and retained example first. Propose a short goal, observable success criteria and the smallest useful scope. Explain consequential choices. Keep this preparation read-only; do not approve or execute work.

presenterNotes: Invite the learner to explain the goal without copying the lesson. Accept their wording rather than rewriting it silently.
The prompt asks for preparation. Copying it does not create or accept a Harness task.

sections.title: Keep one complete useful journey
sections.intro: The first version should read the sample, produce a report and help someone recognize invalid input.
sections.html:
A proposed first-version boundary
IncludeLeave for a later decision
Read the supplied local CSV and validate required values.Remote services and real customer data.
Show all entry, project and category totals.Project filtering or new report calculations.
Produce the agreed readable report.Cloud sync, accounts and deployment.
Explain bad input and avoid a misleading partial report.New dependencies without a reviewed need.

Choose the output you need before preparing a task. The supplied example includes text and HTML output; the agreed task must identify the output being built and checked.

Have the assistant identify the actual files that may change and the inputs and checks that stay protected. Check that its proposed scope fits this first version and preserves unrelated work. A course example does not supply acceptance for a task in your own project.
presenterNotes: Ask whether an excluded feature is essential to this reader. If it is, revise the proposed first version before accepting scope.
Avoid a file-by-file repository tour. The learner needs to understand the allowed effect and protected expected answers.

sections.title: Say how you will recognize success
sections.intro: Use concrete examples and a failure case. A polished appearance alone cannot establish that the totals are right.
sections.html:
• Completeness: all six valid entries appear in the count, without a hidden filter.
  • Totals: the report shows 270 minutes; Orion 180 and Lumen 90.
  • Categories: Development 150, Documentation 75 and Testing 45.
  • Invalid input: an invalid row produces a helpful error and no misleading partial report.
  • Preservation: the input and protected checks remain unchanged.

Ask your assistant to connect each criterion to an independent check. Later you will inspect the actual results and separate review, including concerns the chosen checks may miss.

A saved draft records what you intend. Approval records your decision about the reviewed scope. Starting execution remains a separate action.
presenterNotes: Treat the check as optional discussion. An incorrect choice must not lock navigation.
Use the failure-case requirement to show that success includes an understandable problem path. No new tests are claimed here.

check.question: Which success criterion is useful before the reporting work starts?

options.text: The six supplied entries total 270 minutes, and project totals account for that same total.
options.feedback: This is observable and can be checked independently from the source rows.

options.text: The report looks professional, so its totals can be assumed correct.
options.feedback: Appearance can help the reader, but the totals still need independent checks against the input.

sections.title: Change the reader, then explain the consequence
sections.intro: Suppose a colleague only wants to compare the two projects. Does that require a new feature?
sections.html:
The existing project table already supplies that comparison. A useful next step might be clearer instructions about where to look, rather than adding a filter or rewriting the tool.

Now consider a different request: “Show only Orion's activity.” That changes selection behavior. Keep it as a proposed later change until its goal, permitted files and checks are reviewed.

These practice notes stay in this browser when storage is available. They are not a saved Harness request, approval or execution record. Copy anything important into your actual project brief.

Explain why your chosen scope completes a useful journey. If the existing report already answers the question, keeping the scope unchanged is a valid decision.
presenterNotes: Use less guidance here: ask the learner to distinguish interpreting the report from changing selection behavior.
Preserve the learner’s wording. Browser notes are separate from the saved task and may be unavailable in another browser.

sections.title: Prepare a brief you can review
sections.intro: You are ready for planning when you can explain the goal, the boundary and what would establish success.
sections.html:
Proposed project brief

Reader and benefit
A person reviewing activity wants to explain where the time went.
Input and result
The supplied synthetic CSV becomes the agreed readable activity report.
Success
Six entries; 270 minutes; correct project and category totals; clear bad-input behavior; preserved inputs and checks.
Boundary
A local reporting task. Filtering, remote services and deployment need separate decisions.
Status
Proposed brief, ready for review. It has not accepted or started a new Harness task.

Ask your assistant to prepare the actual request and explain its proposed files and checks. If it uses a form, inspect the whole current request before making its decision.

copies.label: brief handoff prompt
copies.text: Use my reviewed reporting brief to prepare the next planning step. Show the actual goal, current files, proposed allowed changes, protected inputs and independent checks. Explain any unresolved decisions and the current approval point. Preserve my wording and existing work. Stop before accepting scope, starting execution or making provider calls.

presenterNotes: Ask the learner to explain one scope boundary and one success criterion before following the next lesson.
Keep version and observed-learning limits available without making them the main learning task.
